Face the music
féis da miúzik
Accept the unpleasant consequences of what you did — Dar la cara / apechugar.
He had to go in and face the music.
Forms: faces, faced, faced the music.
Get the hang of
guet da jang ov
Learn how to do something with practice — Cogerle el truco a / pillarle el tranquillo.
It takes a week to get the hang of the software.
Forms: gets, got, got the hang of.
Give the benefit of the doubt
guiv da bénefit ov da dáut
Choose to believe someone when you are not sure — Dar el beneficio de la duda.
I'll give him the benefit of the doubt this time.
Pattern: give someone the benefit of the doubt.
Go down the drain
góu dáun da dréin
Be completely wasted — Irse al traste / echarse a perder.
Years of work went down the drain.
Forms: goes, went, gone down the drain.
Hit the road
jit da róud
Leave; set off on a journey — Ponerse en marcha / largarse.
It's late — time to hit the road.
Informal. Forms: hits, hit, hit the road.
In the long run
in da long ran
Over a long period, in the end — A la larga / a largo plazo.
Buying good boots is cheaper in the long run.
Opposite: in the short run.
Keep your fingers crossed
kiip yor fínguers krost
Hope for a good result — Cruzar los dedos.
Keep your fingers crossed for me tomorrow.
Also: fingers crossed, on its own.
Learn the ropes
lern da róups
Learn how a job or system works — Aprender el oficio / coger el tranquillo.
Give her a month to learn the ropes.
From sailing. Also: show someone the ropes.
Lose your touch
luus yor tach
Stop being good at something you used to do well — Perder facultades / perder el toque.
He hasn't lost his touch in the kitchen.
Forms: loses, lost, lost your touch.
Make ends meet
méik ends miit
Have just enough money to live on — Llegar a fin de mes.
With two children it is hard to make ends meet.
Forms: makes, made, made ends meet.
On the same page
on da séim péich
In agreement; understanding the same thing — En la misma onda / de acuerdo.
Let's make sure we're all on the same page.
Used with be. Common at work.
Play devil's advocate
pléi dévils ádvokeit
Argue the other side to test an idea — Hacer de abogado del diablo.
Let me play devil's advocate for a moment.
Often announced before you do it.
Put all your eggs in one basket
put ol yor egs in uán básket
Risk everything on one thing — Jugárselo todo a una carta / poner todos los huevos en la misma cesta.
Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
Nearly always in the negative, as advice.
Read between the lines
riid bituíin da láins
Understand what is meant but not said — Leer entre líneas.
Read between the lines and you'll see he's unhappy.
Forms: reads, read, read between the lines.
Sell like hot cakes
sel láik jot kéiks
Sell very quickly and in large numbers — Venderse como churros / como rosquillas.
The tickets sold like hot cakes.
Forms: sells, sold, sold like hot cakes.
Take it easy
téik it íizi
Relax; do not work too hard — Tomárselo con calma / relajarse.
Take it easy this weekend.
Also a friendly goodbye in American English.
The elephant in the room
di élefant in da ruum
An obvious problem nobody will mention — El elefante en la habitación / lo que nadie se atreve a decir.
Nobody mentioned the elephant in the room: the cost.
Used with be or mention.
Time flies
táim fláis
Time passes surprisingly quickly — El tiempo vuela / cómo pasa el tiempo.
Time flies when you're busy.
Fuller form: time flies when you're having fun.
Turn a blind eye
tern a bláind ái
Deliberately ignore something wrong — Hacer la vista gorda.
The manager turned a blind eye to the lateness.
Pattern: turn a blind eye to something.
Twist someone's arm
tuist sámuans arm
Persuade someone who is reluctant — Convencer a base de insistir / retorcer el brazo.
They twisted my arm and I agreed to sing.
Often joking: you've twisted my arm.
Up to speed
ap tu spiid
Fully informed, or working at the needed level — Al día / puesto al corriente.
Let me bring you up to speed on the project.
Patterns: be up to speed, bring someone up to speed.
Wear your heart on your sleeve
uéer yor jart on yor sliiv
Show your feelings openly — Llevar el corazón en la mano.
He wears his heart on his sleeve.
Forms: wears, wore, worn your heart on your sleeve.
When pigs fly
uén pigs flái
Never — Cuando las ranas críen pelo.
He'll apologise when pigs fly.
Sarcastic. Also: when hell freezes over.
A close call
a klóus kol
A narrow escape from danger — Por poco / un buen susto.
That was a close call with the cyclist.
Also: a close shave, a near miss.
Around the clock
aráund da klok
All day and all night without stopping — Las veinticuatro horas / sin parar.
Crews worked around the clock to clear the road.
Also an adjective: round-the-clock care.
At the drop of a hat
at da drop ov a jat
Immediately, without needing persuasion — A la mínima / sin pensárselo.
She'd move abroad at the drop of a hat.
Goes at the end of the sentence.
Bite off more than you can chew
báit of mor dan yu kan chuu
Take on more than you can manage — Abarcar más de lo que se puede apretar.
Three jobs at once? You're biting off more than you can chew.
Forms: bites, bit, bitten off more than you can chew.
Cross that bridge when you come to it
kros dat brich uén yu kam tu it
Deal with a problem only when it happens — Cruzar ese puente cuando llegues / ya se verá.
We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
Said to stop someone worrying early.
Get a grip
guet a grip
Take control of yourself — Controlarse / centrarse.
Get a grip — it's only a game.
Informal; can sound sharp.
Give someone a hand
guiv sámuan a jand
Help someone — Echar una mano a.
Could you give me a hand with this box?
Also: give someone a hand, meaning applaud.
In a nutshell
in a nátshel
In very few words — En pocas palabras / en resumen.
In a nutshell, we cannot afford it.
Goes at the start of the sentence.
Jump the gun
yamp da gan
Act too soon — Precipitarse / adelantarse.
They jumped the gun and announced it early.
From athletics. Forms: jumps, jumped, jumped the gun.
Keep it under your hat
kiip it ánder yor jat
Keep something secret — Guardar el secreto / no decir ni mu.
I'm leaving in May, but keep it under your hat.
Said when telling someone a secret.
Let bygones be bygones
let báigons bi báigons
Forgive and forget an old quarrel — Borrón y cuenta nueva / lo pasado, pasado.
They agreed to let bygones be bygones.
A fixed phrase; never changed.
Lose your head
luus yor jed
Panic and stop thinking clearly — Perder la cabeza / perder los nervios.
Don't lose your head if the alarm goes off.
Forms: loses, lost, lost your head.
Not my cup of tea
not mai kap ov tii
Not the kind of thing you like — No es lo mío / no me va.
Opera isn't really my cup of tea.
Almost always in the negative, and polite.
On a shoestring
on a shúustring
With very little money — Con cuatro perras / con un presupuesto mínimo.
They travelled around Asia on a shoestring.
Also an adjective: a shoestring budget.
Out of hand
áut ov jand
Out of control — Fuera de control / descontrolado.
The party got out of hand.
Also: reject something out of hand, meaning at once.
Second to none
sékond tu nan
Better than everything else — Insuperable / sin igual.
Their bread is second to none.
Used with be. A strong compliment.
Sleep on it
sliip on it
Wait until tomorrow before deciding — Consultarlo con la almohada.
Don't answer now — sleep on it.
Forms: sleeps, slept, slept on it.
Take the bull by the horns
téik da bul bai da jorns
Face a difficulty boldly — Coger el toro por los cuernos.
She took the bull by the horns and spoke to him.
Word for word the same in Spanish.
Under the wire
ánder da uáir
Only just in time — En el último momento / por los pelos.
The application got in under the wire.
American English. From horse racing.
Have a lot on your plate
jav a lot on yor pléit
Have a great deal to deal with — Tener mucho entre manos / ir hasta arriba.
I can't help this week — I have a lot on my plate.
Also: have enough on your plate.
Cost a fortune
kost a fórchun
Be very expensive — Costar una fortuna / un dineral.
Those tickets cost a fortune.
Forms: costs, cost, cost a fortune.
